entries.title: Germany news: Sick leave wage bill doubles in 15 years
entries.summary: German firms paid out a record €86 billion in wages to employees on sick leave last year, according to new research. Meanwhile, dozens of firefighters tackled a blaze at a refugee home in Berlin overnight. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Sick leave wage bill doubles in 15 years

Published August 29, 2026last updated August 29, 2026

German firms paid out a record €86 billion in wages to employees on sick leave last year, according to new research. Meanwhile, dozens of firefighters tackled a blaze at a refugee home in Berlin overnight. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German firms faced a record sick-leave wage bill last year of €86 billion
  • Lower Saxony's state premier calls for deal on Volkswagen restructuring
  • Hundreds of people were evacuated from a fire at a Berlin refugee shelter
  • A Taliban team is in Germany to facilitate Afghan deportations, according to a media report
  • AfD youth wing rejects party plans to leave the euro currency

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, August 29, and Sunday, August 30.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010

Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010

The total amount of wages German firms paid in sick and maternity leave has more than doubled over the past 15 years, a study from the Cologne-based German Economic Institute (IW) shows.

IW estimated that German companies paid a record-high €85.6 billion ($111 billion) in wages to employees who were out sick last year. This compares to €36.9 billion in 2010.

Of the larger figure, €72.5 billion represented gross wages, while €13.1 billion was earmarked for social security contributions.

IW said several factors have contributed to the rise, including wage hikes and inflation in other employee costs.

The institute said the total number of employed people has also grown since 2010, meaning more workers are eligible for sick leave.

IW, however, said it had noted a "significant" rise in recorded sick leave since Germany moved to electronic medical certificates in 2022.

Separate research by the Berlin-based IGES Institute in January showed that German workers now take an average of 19.5 working days as sick leave per year, a noticeable increase from about 13 days in 2018.

In an effort to stem the rise, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government will from January ban patients from receiving sick notes from doctors by phone. 

In Germany, employers are generally required to pay workers' salaries for up to six weeks before the statutory health insurance fund takes over by paying sickness benefits.

Skip next section Lower Saxony premier seeks deal on VW restructuring

Lower Saxony premier seeks deal on VW restructuring

Volkswagen's second-biggest shareholder has called on all sides to agree on a restructuring plan for the German auto giant in the next few days.

Olaf Lies, state premier of Lower Saxony — which holds 18% of VW's shareholder voting rights — said he was convinced "a viable solution" can be found.

"I strongly urge that we ​use the time remaining until the next meeting to bring the different positions together," Lies told journalists on Friday.

The state leader noted that VW must face its numerous business challenges head-on, namely costly tariffs, falling demand and intense competition from China.

But he said the group's position in Germany's industrial landscape ‌also had to be considered.

"With its sites in Lower Saxony and ‌across ​Germany, its tens of thousands of employees and their families, and its suppliers and service providers, Volkswagen also bears an enormous responsibility for the wider economy and society," Lies said.

VW's management now thinks they may need to cut up to 100,000 jobs and that several German factories may face closure.

The supervisory board of Europe's largest automaker is due to meet on September 4 ‌to discuss a ⁠turnaround ⁠plan.

Skip next section Survey: Trump's return increased US influence over Germany

Survey: Trump's return increased US influence over Germany

Two-thirds of residents think the United States has more influence on Germany since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House.

A poll by the Forsa research institute found that 67% of respondents agreed, while just 11% thought there was less US influence. Around 18% thought it was the same.

The survey for the German-language Internationale Politik (International Politics) magazine found only 2% of 18 to 29-year-olds and 6% of 30 to 44-year-olds think US influence in Germany is lower than before Trump's second term. That's versus 18% of respondents aged 60 and over.

Germany-US ties have soured since Trump's reelection, due to surprise tariffs, talk of seizing Greenland and open sniping over Russia's war in Ukraine and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.

Skip next section Report: Taliban team in Berlin to aid Afghan deportations

Report: Taliban team in Berlin to aid Afghan deportations

The Taliban  has sent a team of three people to Germany to help facilitate the deportation of Afghan nationals, public broadcaster NDR reported.

NDR said the delegation arrived in Germany on Wednesday and is staying at the Afghan embassy in Berlin.

The broadcaster said their mission is to provide documents recognized by the Taliban in Kabul to Afghan nationals being deported from Germany.

The delegation is also due to spend time in Bonn and Munich, where Afghanistan  has consulates general.

The arrival of the delegation is contentious as Germany — along with most of the rest of the world — does not recognize the Taliban government.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz calls the contacts a purely technical necessity to return people with no right to stay.

Critics, however, say his government is legitimizing the Taliban to help raise deportation numbers.

Germany suspended deportations to Afghanistan when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

They resumed three years later, initially for convicted criminals.

According to German government data, 15,343 Afghan nationals in Germany are required to leave the country, as of the end of June, including more than 1,500 children.

Skip next section AfD youth wing: Germany shouldn't leave euro

AfD youth wing: Germany shouldn't leave euro

The youth wing of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has broken ranks with party leadership and called for Germany not to leave the euro currency.

"We do not want Germany to leave the euro, but to address the existing structural flaws in the euro system," Jean-Pascal Hohm, head of the Generation Deutschland (GD) youth organization, told the Bild newspaper.

The GD is due to adopt a position on the issue at a conference in the city of Magdeburg on Saturday.

A draft statement says the euro has strengthened the European single market but has "structural flaws," and calls for reforms that would improve stability without giving up Europe's economic unity.

In its 2025 election manifesto, the euroskeptic AfD has called for Germany to leave the euro, the single currency of 21 EU member states.

The GD was established last year as the AfD's new youth organization after the party dissolved its previous youth wing, the Junge Alternative (JA), after it was labeled right-wing extremist by intelligence officials.

Skip next section Hundreds evacuated affter blaze at Berlin refugee shelter

Hundreds evacuated affter blaze at Berlin refugee shelter

A fire broke out early Saturday morning at a refugee shelter in Berlin-Spandau, a borough on the outer western edge of Germany's capital.

The dpa news agency reported that the blaze broke out on the fourth floor of a six-story building, designed to accommodate about 1,200 people

Citing the fire department, dpa said furnishings caught fire in the hallway for reasons yet to be determined.

The smoke then spread to the fifth and sixth floors.

Four people were treated for smoke inhalation, the statement said. Three were taken to hospital.

Several hundred residents were evacuated from the shelter, with between 50 and 60 people moved to alternative accommodation.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning from Bonn, where the Rhine River water level is creeping back up after hitting a low earlier this month during the drought.

Overnight, a fire at a refugee center in Berlin forced the evacuation of hundreds of residents.

A report by public broadcaster NDR reveals that the Taliban has sent a delegation to Germanyto help facilitate the deportation of Afghan nationals, whose asylum claims have been rejected.

Also, while the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) wants to leave the euro currency, the party's youth wing has spoken out against the policy, calling instead for "structural flaws" in the euro system to be fixed. 

Here you'll find our coverage of the latest news, sport and analysis from across Germany this weekend.

entries.title: Russian strike on warehouse near Kyiv kills dozens
entries.summary: Hundreds were also forced to evacuate after a Russian attack on a warehouse near Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, sparked a huge fire and explosions.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Russian strike on warehouse near Kyiv kills dozens

August 29, 2026

Hundreds were also forced to evacuate after a Russian attack on a warehouse near Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, sparked a huge fire and explosions.

A Russian drone strike on a warehouse near Kyiv late Friday has killed at least 37 people, Ukrainian authorities said.

"Unfortunately, the death toll in the Bucha district has risen to 37," Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko said in a post on Telegram on Saturday.

Among those killed was Taras Didych, head of the Dmytrivka community, who was one of the first to rush to the scene to rescue people, Tkachenko earlier said.

It had previously been reported that more than 40 people had been injured.

In recent months, Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes, increasingly hitting civilian infrastructure such as logistics warehouses and oil and port facilities. These attacks have resulted in more civilian casualties. 

What else do we know about the Russian drone attack near Kyiv?

The strike sparked a major fire and explosions at the warehouse in the Bucha district, close to the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, forcing more than 370 people to evacuate the region.

In a statement on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that "a warehouse was struck, followed by a detonation," and that nearby infrastructure suffered "significant damage."

He also said that criminal proceedings had been opened on charges of official negligence.

"There are regulations in place — ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," Zelenskyy said.

Kyiv under jet-powered drone attacks

Friday's drone attack followed ​two days of constant air raids aimed at the Ukrainian capital and the surrounding region.

"Kyiv is under virtually nonstop attack from jet-powered drones. Ukraine cannot be left alone in finding solutions to defend against such strikes," said Zelenskyy.

It's been more than four and a half years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbor.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: US, Ecuador forces strike alleged drug smuggling boat
entries.summary: Tackling drug trafficking in Latin America is a key priority for Washington. In March, Ecuador joined a US-led coalition to combat the drug trade in the region.
entries.content:
August 29, 2026

Tackling drug trafficking in Latin America is a key priority for Washington. In March, Ecuador joined a US-led coalition to combat the drug trade in the region.

The US military said on Friday it had destroyed an alleged drug trafficking boat in a coordinated operation with Ecuador.

In a post on X, US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said that its forces intercepted a vessel "operating as a floating refueling station" in the Eastern Pacific.

According to SOUTHCOM, the vessel was operating "in support of the Los Choneros violent narco-terrorist organization," referring to one of Ecuador's most powerful criminal gangs, which Washington has designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organization.

"Working together with our Ecuadorian partners, our coalition dealt a decisive blow to a narco-terrorist operation responsible for moving significant amounts of drugs through the region," SOUTHCOM said.

US, Ecuador combat drug cartels

In March, Ecuador joined President Donald Trump's "Shield of the Americas" — a US-led coalition focused on combating drug trafficking across the region.

Ecuador's strategic location between Colombia and Peru — the world's two largest producers of cocaine — makes the country a key transit hub for drug-trafficking gangs.

The US military launched Operation Southern Spear in September 2025 as part of a fight against drug trafficking in the region.

The Trump administration, however, has not presented definitive evidence that the vessels targeted in its operations were carrying or transporting illegal drugs. 

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Death toll from Nepal-Tibet floods rises to over 600
entries.summary: Heavy rain is complicating an already difficult rescue effort, as hundreds remain missing three days after deadly flash floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border region.
entries.content:
Nepal

Death toll from Nepal-Tibet floods rises to over 600

August 29, 2026

Heavy rain is complicating an already difficult rescue effort, as hundreds remain missing three days after deadly flash floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border region.

The latest death toll from the devastating flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border was reported on Saturday to be over 600, as frantic rescue operations to search for hundreds of missing people entered a fourth day.

According to Nepal's disaster agency, the death toll in Nepal now stands at 626, with 2,426 people — including foreigners — still missing.

Across the border in Tibet, China's state news agency, Xinhua, has confirmed seven deaths and reported 554 missing individuals.

A glacial collapse on Wednesday sent rock, ice, mud and debris surging through the Himalayan mountain river systems below.

The flood swept through areas near the Chinese border, ravaging entire towns and damaging hydropower plants.

What is the status of rescue efforts in Nepal?

Rainy weather conditions are hindering aerial rescue operations in Nepal.

Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told the media on Saturday that helicopter operations were on hold until the weather improved.

Rescuers are battling thick layers of mud in the affected areas, which is making it difficult for helicopters to land and take off.

Tunnels in the mountainous region are also a challenge, Basnet said.

The army has located people trapped in a tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project in Nepal's Rasuwa District. Over 100 people are believed to be inside the tunnel filled with mud.

Basnet said that rescuers were struggling to locate the entry points of the tunnel and had made use of baskets and ropes to reach some people. There are also limited places for helicopters to land in the area.

On Friday, Nepal's Army shared visuals of some people being rescued from the tunnel. The survivors were seen stuck in the mud, while officials crawled through the sludge and held out their hands to them.

Nepalese authorities said that the bodies of many flood victims have also been found dozens of kilometers from the disaster zone in Chitwan District in southern Nepal, which borders India.

Meanwhile, Indian authorities said they recovered the bodies of seven people who were swept downstream from Nepal and believe them to be flood victims.

Nepal needs help in technical areas, says foreign minister

Late on Friday, Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told the Reuters news agency that his country needed equipment, along with technical knowledge in tunnel rescue operations.

Khanal also told Reuters that Nepal did not need help with search and rescue operations but needed assistance in opening transport and communication lines in places where bridges were destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storage of bodies for a longer timeframe.

"We have already made requests for such ⁠specialized ​services and technical assistance in areas where we don't have enough expertise and technical know-how," ​Reuters quoted Khanal as saying.

Nepal's Foreign Ministry had on Friday declined foreign involvement in search and rescue.

Nepal's post-flood rebuilding estimated at $4-$5 billion

In another Reuters interview, Nepal's Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said that the Himalayan nation may need $4 billion (€3.5 billion) ⁠to $5 billion ⁠to rebuild after the flood.

The estimate is equivalent ​to nearly a tenth of Nepal's economy.

"The initial estimate is ​between $4-$5 billion. Just an estimate," Wagle told Reuters, adding that the bill would be much less than what was needed in reconstruction after the disastrous 2015 earthquake — Nepal's worst ‌ recorded disaster.

"Loss and damage is being assessed," he said.

What do we know about rescue operations in Tibet?

In Gyirong, one of the hardest-hit areas in Tibet along the China-Nepal border, Beijing had temporarily halted its rescue efforts due to the risk of renewed flooding before announcing that the threat had waned.

China's Xinhua agency reported on Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the Gyirong area.

The glacial collapse on Wednesday led to the formation of a barrier lake upstream due to debris dams. Experts warned that the lake had started to overflow.

On Saturday, Chinese authorities announced that the lake had begun to shrink.

China's state broadcaster, CCTV, cited the Ministry of Water Resources as saying that satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake in the Tsangpo River basin on Saturday morning showed a reduction of around 21,000 square meters compared to images from Thursday.

Authorities have also identified a larger body of water at the bottom of the glacier collapse.

"We estimate its area to be over 120,000 ⁠square ​meters, but its depth is currently unknown," Reuters quoted Chen Hongqi, a senior engineer at ​the Ministry of Natural Resources' Geological Disaster Technical Guidance Center, as saying.

Reuters also reported an official of Nepal's Disaster ​Management Authority as saying that flood risks will remain until the two lakes have fully drained.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: South Korea leans toward military conscription for women
entries.summary: Facing a population decline, fewer potential service members and calls for social equality to be extended to national military service, Korea is inching closer to breaking the taboo on women on the front line.
entries.content:
South Korea

South Korea leans toward military conscription for women

August 29, 2026

Facing a population decline, fewer potential service members and calls for social equality to be extended to national military service, Korea is inching closer to breaking the taboo on women on the front line.

Nearly 60% of South Koreans are now in favor of young women serving mandatory military service alongside their male counterparts, according to a recent survey, representing a significant shift in the long-held taboo against women being obliged to defend the nation.

Thousands of women already serve in the South Korean armed forces on a voluntary basis, but the debate over mandatory service has always been delicate.

Now, for a series of reasons that include a falling birth rate and shrinking number of recruits as well as an insistence that social equality means that women should also serve, the issue has re-emerged ahead of a reform of the national defense plan scheduled to be released this autumn.

Yet, there are still those who insist women should be kept away from the front lines and, instead, that South Korea should invest more in drones and other advanced technologies.

"South Korea's male-centered conscription system has long been closely connected to traditional gender roles," said Hyobin Lee, a professor at Sogang University in Seoul.

"Men were generally expected to protect the country and the family and to fight in wartime, while women were expected to take primary responsibility for childbirth, childcare and the household," she told DW.

A second factor is the intensifying debate about gender equality, a debate in large part driven by young men, she said.

Warfare moves beyond the physical

"South Korean men generally perform their military service in their early 20s, which interrupts their education, employment or early career development," Lee said.

"At the same time, gender equality has become an increasingly important social value, and women's opportunities in education and employment have expanded."

"As a result, some younger men ask a very simple question: If society expects equality in rights and opportunities, why does one of the country's most significant civic obligations — military service — still fall only on men?"

Another contributing factor is the change in the nature of the military itself, with a shift away from physically demanding combat roles that were perceived as being more suited to men and the emergence of a national defense more heavily reliant on technology.

This includes unmanned systems, cyber capabilities, information and communications technology and others that do not require physical strength.

What does the study show?

According to the study, carried out by the Reform Institute, the policy research arm of the conservative-leaning Reform Party, and published on August 20, almost 60% of the respondents were in favor of changing the law to require women to undergo national service. Just 34% were opposed to the idea.

Nearly 65% of men were in favor — a figure that rose to 71.7% among men in their 20s and 30s — with 54.5% of women across all age groups similarly supportive.

At present, all able-bodied men are required to complete a minimum of 18 months and up to 21 months of service and can be called back into service in the event of a national emergency, such as war breaking out on the tense Korean Peninsula.

The latest figures highlight, however, personnel shortages that have affected South Korea's armed forces.

According to the Defense Ministry, around 332,000 men were eligible to perform mandatory military service in 2019. That number fell to 257,000 men in 2022 and is forecast to shrink to just 120,000 men in 2043.

While Hyobin Lee is strongly in favor of equality throughout South Korean society, she fears that obliging women to serve the same military terms as men may turn out to be a negative because so many other elements in society still lag.

Women's traditional responsibilities remain unchanged

"Women in South Korea still bear a much greater share of the responsibilities associated with pregnancy, childbirth and childcare," she underlined.

"Having a child can still lead to career interruption or withdrawal from the labor market, and women's responsibilities for caregiving have not declined to the same extent that their participation in education and employment has increased," Lee added.

"If women were also required to complete military service, the cumulative burden across their life course could become even greater," she pointed out.

"In a country that is already experiencing an extremely low birth rate, it is also possible that this additional compulsory obligation could further delay or discourage marriage and childbirth."

Lee comes from a family with a strong military background, with a grandfather an admiral in the navy and her father serving in the same branch of the military.

But she would have had reservations in completing mandatory service herself.

"If someone chooses a military career, that is completely different from compulsory service," she said.

"Eighteen months in your 20s is a very significant period in a person's life. It is a time when people are studying, beginning their careers, and making important personal choices. Having to put all of that on hold because the state requires it is a substantial burden," she said.

"Personally, I would have found it extremely difficult to give up 18 months of my younger years in that way."

Song Young-Chae, a Seoul-based academic and human rights activist, completed two years in the infantry as a younger man, when periods of service were longer. He is opposed to mandatory service for women.

"The defense of the nation is traditionally the responsibility of men, and I do not believe that there is such an urgent need to conscript women into front-line service," he told DW.

Need to invest in modern technology

"I served along the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) with North Korea, and it was a hard posting," he added. "I believe that we should be investing far more in drones, robots and other advanced military technologies to protect our borders."

The South Korean government set up a task force in 2025 to revise the nation's basic defense plan, with troop modernization and an overhaul of the conscription system — introduced in the 1950s — high on the agenda.

In an interview with the Yonhap News Agency on August 9, Military Manpower Commissioner Hong So-young admitted that the nation faces a "demographic cliff" and that reforms are urgently required. Those include potentially reducing the number of people exempt from service and requiring foreign-born people who have taken South Korean nationality to also serve.

Hong made no comment about mandatory service for Korean women, but said the system needs a "fundamental" overhaul.

Edited by: Shamil Shams

entries.title: This extremely successful author polarizes German readers
entries.summary: She's young and she says what she thinks: Caroline Wahl is topping Germany's bestseller lists with her novels. But she has also faced public backlash.
entries.content:
August 29, 2026

She's young and she says what she thinks: Caroline Wahl is topping Germany's bestseller lists with her novels. But she has also faced public backlash.

Caroline Wahl, 31, has published three novels to date. All three shot to the top of Germany's fiction bestseller lists.

Now, her fourth book is set to be released on August 28: "1999 Meter über dem Meer" (1999 Meters Above Sea) tells the story of a young woman who takes on a false identity to mingle among the high society in St. Moritz, Switzerland.

It is one of the most anticipated new books of the summer in Germany.

So what is the secret to Caroline Wahl's success?

Debut with a bang

Caroline Wahl's breakthrough came with her first novel, from 2023: "22 Bahnen" (22 Lengths) sold more than a million copies in German-language editions.

The story of the young student Tilda, who has to navigate everyday life alongside her alcoholic mother and her little sister, was praised by critics for its straightforward, modern writing style.

What's more, the novel managed to fascinate readers across generations: It includes references to contemporary pop culture as well as to classic literature.

"The many references make the novels both diverse and ambiguous," says Matthias Schaffrick, a research associate at the Collaborative Research Center "Transformations of the Popular" at the University of Siegen, who recently organized a two-day symposium on Wahl's works.

"What stands out most is how she experiments with different narrative styles and questions them, instead of simply telling a story," Shaffrick tells DW. "This opens up a literary space with multiple possibilities, enabling different interpretations and certainly contributing to the appeal of her novels for many readers."

Polarizing ambition

The success led to the media becoming interested in the young author, and quickly showed that Caroline Wahl does not care much for conventions: She speaks her mind freely and doesn't mind facing backlash. "I enjoy being polarizing," she told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper last weekend. "I like that there's no gray area, people either hate me, and then they really hate me (...). Or they like me."

In the podcast "Hotel Matze," she said she wanted to become one of Germany's most famous authors. Her words quickly created a stir, but Wahl didn't mind: "I'm really not up for false modesty. It's not wrong to state your goals ambitiously," she said on the arts and culture TV show "Twist" on the Arte channel. "For young women in particular, it's more extreme than for men — people get irritated when a young woman says, 'I want to be the best.' I want to change that with my attitude."     

A passion for fast cars

Part of that is openly speaking about enjoying her newfound wealth. In an interview with SZ-Magazin, she said: "It's not only the writing that is enjoyable, but also being successful. Financial success is also important." She loves fast cars, drives a convertible and bought a camper van she likes to park somewhere with a view of the sea to work.

On social media, she faced a lot of criticism. She has been accused of making money off the literary depiction of poverty in "22 Bahnen," despite never having lived an impoverished life herself. It's an age-old discussion about whether authors are only allowed to write about things they have experienced themselves. Wahl replied to this criticism on the Deutschlandfunk radio station, explaining that above all, writing to her means "exploring spaces that I don't know and feeling empathy for people who live a different life than mine."

But even without the debate on her credibility, a young woman who speaks openly about material success still seems to be unsettling for many people in Germany — men and women alike — as the many negative reactions show. To Wahl herself, the debate is misogynist.

On Instagram, she wrote a caption for a photo of her light blue BMW: "I find it weird and don't quite get why it's cool for rappers or other men to show off their AMGs, etc., but when a woman author wants to buy a sports car (and can afford to do so!!!), people advise her not to do it and more importantly, not to show it in public."

Author and influencer

"What happens when something becomes very popular?" asks literary scholar Matthias Schaffrick: "The popularity starts being scrutinized, which you can observe in Caroline Wahl's case. And we can see what it means to be a popular author. It's not only her novels that play a role, but also the persona she creates for herself as an author."

By being active on Instagram, where she has even tested energy drinks, she also taps into the role of an influencer, says Matthias Schaffrick. "It makes her even more popular and offers new topics for conversation. At the same time, the public debate shifts the focus away from her literature, which is what's actually interesting about the Caroline Wahl phenomenon."

Wahl herself admits that the intensity of the backlash and criticism has hurt her. In an interview with the SWR TV channel, she explained that social criticism is not necessarily her intention. "I'm not trying to change anything with my stories. Above all, I want to tell stories."

'22 Lengths' on school curricula

When it comes to best‑sellers, opinions always differ among German literary critics: Is this entertaining literature, or serious literature with high artistic aspirations? The arts and feature sections of numerous newspapers come to different conclusions on whether Caroline Wahl's novels can be classified as part of the latter. In an interview with Spiegel, Wahl said she finds "drawing a line between entertaining and serious simply annoying."

So far, Wahl's novels have not been nominated for the German Book Prize, Germany's highest literature award. In 2024, the writer voiced her disappointment in typical fashion on Instagram: "I'm sad and angry that I have not been included on the longlist, even if I somehow knew this would happen. Too successful, says my agent."

Back then, her debut novel could have been included on the list — a book that was quickly added to school curricula and has now been made into a film.

Likewise, on this year's longlist, Wahl's novel "Die Assistentin" (The Assistant) has not been included. A literature critic from Frankfurter Rundschau had this to say about the decision: "Why is good literature always supposed to hurt before it can be deemed 'valuable'? (...) The fact that an author like Wahl has been ignored, simply because her captivating writing fascinates millions of readers, makes me really angry."

Presumably, Caroline Wahl's fans will ensure that her new novel becomes another bestseller — even without the German Book Prize.

entries.title: Serbia: Keeping EU, Russia in play ahead of key election
entries.summary: As Serbia heads towards an uncertain election, President Aleksandar Vucic is balancing ties with Russia and EU ambitions. But growing geopolitical tensions and pressure at home are narrowing his room to maneuver.
entries.content:
Serbia

Serbia: Keeping EU, Russia in play ahead of key election

August 29, 2026

As Serbia heads towards an uncertain election, President Aleksandar Vucic is balancing ties with Russia and EU ambitions. But growing geopolitical tensions and pressure at home are narrowing his room to maneuver.

Smoke from the wildfires still hangs over parts of Serbia, but as the flames slowly recede, another debate is taking shape in their wake — one that has less to do with firefighting and more with politics.

In early August, wildfires swept across Serbia, affecting more than 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) in the Deliblato Sands Special Nature Reserve alone. For days, firefighters, soldiers and helicopters battled the flames.

Then a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 firefighting aircraft arrived in the southern city of Nis. Serbia had turned to Moscow for help, making Russia the first foreign country it asked to provide a firefighting aircraft. Pro-government media greeted its arrival with celebratory coverage, dubbing the aircraft the "Russian beast."

"Considering that there are no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the European Union, the arriving Russian aircraft will significantly strengthen our capacities to fight the fires," said Luka Causic, head of the Serbian Interior Ministry's Department for Emergency Situations.

A pragmatic choice between EU, Russia — or a political signal?

The episode, however, was already being viewed through a geopolitical lens, as Serbia had sought Russian assistance before activating the EU's emergency mechanism.

When it did, the response was swift. Brussels mobilized four helicopters from its strategic rescEU reserve, based in Czechia, Romania and Slovakia, along with ground firefighting teams from Germany and Romania.

Vucic rejected the idea that turning to Russia first was a foreign-policy decision or a sign of Serbia's political alignment with Moscow.

"As far as equipment and resources are concerned, we are a European giant. The helicopters we received from Europe to fight the fires are less capable than ours and have a lower carrying capacity than our own," Vucic said during a visit to the Deliblato Sands.

Zelenskyy in Belgrade

The wildfire episode came less than two weeks after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy made his first official visit to Serbia.

The two presidents reaffirmed their support for each other's territorial integrity, which is particularly significant for Belgrade because Ukraine does not recognise Kosovo's independence.

But Vucic is also trying to keep the other side on board, says Vuk Vuksanovic, a political scientist and foreign-policy lecturer at King's College London.

Vuksanovic argues that Vucic's engagement with Zelenskyy must therefore be portrayed in Moscow not as a fundamental shift in Serbia's relationship with Russia, but as a response to Western pressure and Serbia's own interests.

"Vucic is now trying to make sure that neither the West nor Russia becomes an open opponent during the election campaign," said Vuksanovic.

"Zelenskyy was primarily received so that the ruling coalition could present itself to Europeans as a great friend of Ukraine. In the same way, Vucic is trying to present himself to the Trump administration as a great friend of Israel, primarily to ensure that neither the European Union nor the United States becomes an opponent of the ruling party during the election campaign," Vuksanovic added.

Vucic's room for maneuver is shrinking

The problem is that the room to maintain these relationships may be shrinking.

The deeper the confrontation between Russia and the West becomes, the harder it is for Serbia to remain close to both without facing pressure to choose.

The European Union increasingly expects candidate countries to align their foreign and security policies with those of the bloc. Serbia's refusal to impose sanctions on Russia remains one of the most visible obstacles to closer alignment.

But Moscow, too, has reasons not to take Belgrade's loyalty for granted, Vuksanovic said. He argues that Russia does not fully trust Vucic, even as Moscow continues to support his narrative about "color revolutions" —  a reference to anti-government protests, in this case the student-led protests in Serbia that started last year, which Vucic and Russia portray as Western-backed attempts to destabilize the government.

For Vucic, however, the longer-term question of Serbia's ties with Russia can wait. The more immediate question is whether he will survive the election, tentatively scheduled for October, and remain in a position to preserve that delicate balance himself.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

entries.title: Iceland holds knife-edge referendum on EU membership talks
entries.summary: The Nordic nation shelved earlier plans to join the EU over fishing rights, but geopolitics, including Trump's threat to seize Greenland, has prompted a rethink.
entries.content:
Iceland

Iceland holds knife-edge referendum on EU membership talks

August 29, 2026

The Nordic nation shelved earlier plans to join the EU over fishing rights, but geopolitics, including Trump's threat to seize Greenland, has prompted a rethink.

Iceland holds a national referendum on Saturday on whether to restart negotiations to join the European Union.

The Nordic nation has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming the bloc’s 28th member.

Iceland's left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a vote next year but brought it forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.

What do we know about Iceland's referendum?

As they head to one of hundreds of polling stations, voters will be asked a simple yes/no question:

Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?

The question relates to a previous attempt by the Icelandic government to join the EU in 2009, at the height of the global financial crisis that devastated the local economy. The accession plan was later shelved.

Saturday's vote is described as too close to call, with a Gallup poll on Friday suggesting a narrow majority of Icelanders oppose reopening talks. Other recent polls suggest a narrow lead for the yes vote.

Although Iceland has never been an EU member, it is already closely integrated with the bloc.

It is a member of both the European Economic Area (EEA) — which gives access to the EU's frictionless single market — and the Schengen Area free-travel zone.

Of Iceland's roughly 400,000 population, around 265,000 are eligible to vote.

What are the deciding factors among voters?

Voters have grown increasingly concerned about geopolitics, including the threat from Russia and US President Donald Trump's threats to seize nearby Greenland from Denmark.

Icelanders, who gained independence from Denmark in 1944, have been asking whether they could be next.

"We can't really trust the US anymore," said Hildur Knutsdottir, a horror fiction writer who plans to vote in favor of EU membership.

Arctic nations sit at the center of a growing contest for the polar north, as the United States, Russia and China jostle for influence over sea routes, natural resources and security.

The left-leaning Icelandic coalition believes EU membership could help counter Trump's ambitions in the North Atlantic.

"The international order that underpinned our security and prosperity for decades is under serious pressure," Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Gunnarsdottir told Reuters last week.

"In times like these, small nations need to ​think carefully about where they stand and who stands with them," she added.

Fishing, interest rates and national identity

The last attempt to join the EU was shelved in 2015 largely over concerns about joining the bloc's common fisheries policy.

Icelanders have been living off hefty cod and haddock catches for centuries and are loath to open the chilled Arctic waters to Spanish, Dutch and other EU trawlers, which is a requirement from Brussels.

The government has said it could try to negotiate a full opt-out from the policy.

Some economists think Icelanders, who have struggled under high inflation and interest rates, could benefit financially from EU membership and possibly the adoption of the euro.

National identity is another driver of voting, with opponents of EU membership noting how Iceland enjoys all the benefits of European integration without being a full member.

"For a country like ours with our small economy, it's very important to maintain our sovereignty and not to transfer more power than we would have to do to the EU," former Prime Minister Katrin Jakobsdottir said at an ​event in Reykjavik ‌on Thursday.

What happens if Iceland votes to restart EU talks?

A yes vote would trigger a negotiating process with the EU's executive branch, the European Commission.

This would involve discussions on 35 areas, from the economy to human rights.

A foreign ministry memo estimates accession talks could start by the end of the year and take 18 to 24 months.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: India news: PM Modi leaves for Central Asian tour
entries.summary: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is traveling to Uzbekistan for a two-day state visit, after which he will go to Kyrgyzstan for the SCO Summit. Meanwhile, hundreds of Indians are still missing in Nepal. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: PM Modi leaves for Central Asian tour

Published August 29, 2026last updated August 29, 2026

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is traveling to Uzbekistan for a two-day state visit, after which he will go to Kyrgyzstan for the SCO Summit. Meanwhile, hundreds of Indians are still missing in Nepal. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is traveling to Uzbekistan for bilateral talks
  • Hundreds of Indians remain missing in Nepal floods
  • Indian opposition claims Sonia Gandhi's memoir dropped by Penguin India over Modi, RSS and China
  • Controversial Hindu nationalist group chief Mohan Bhagwat set to deliver speech in NYC

Here are the biggest headlines from India on Saturday, August 29, and Sunday, August 30. 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section WATCH — Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the EU dispute

WATCH — Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the EU dispute

The fight over basmati rice has become one of the most complex disputes in the global food trade.

Both India and Pakistan claim the premium, aromatic rice as part of their agriculture and cultural heritage, and both are seeking European Union recognition for its geographical origin.

But years after the first application was filed in 2018, the EU has yet to decide how the name should be protected and by whom.

Basmati is among the world's most valuable rice varieties, generating significant export revenues and carrying strong historical ties to the Punjab region, which spans both countries.

Meanwhile, experts warn that widespread misuse of the name on international markets could undermine future protection altogether. As Brussels weighs its options, the outcome could have far-reaching consequences.

Skip next section Congress slams Penguin India for backing out of Sonia Gandhi's memoir

Congress slams Penguin India for backing out of Sonia Gandhi's memoir

Leaders of India's largest opposition party, the Indian National Congress (INC), alleged that publishing house Penguin India was pressured to back out of publishing veteran politician Sonia Gandhi's memoir due to portions related to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist group, and China's alleged occupation of Indian territory under Modi's rule.

Sonia Gandhi has been a leading figure in Indian politics for decades. She was the president of the INC from 1998 to 2017 and is the party's longest-serving chief.

Earlier this month, Alfred A. Knopf announced that Gandhi's "Belonging: A Journey of Love" will be published on November 10. Knopf is a publishing imprint under Penguin Random House.

"Suppressing the book of Sonia Gandhi, a person of such stature, a senior leader of the nation, and former Leader of the Opposition, under pressure is tantamount to the murder of freedom of Expression," senior INC leader Ashok gehlot said in a post on X.

"The real issue is that pressure was put on Penguin India to remove the portions related to Modi, the RSS, and the occupation of Indian territory by China during Modi's rule. This is the murder of democracy," he said.

In another post, Gehlot said "there's some kind of pressure. It could be from the PMO [Prime Minister's Office] or someone else — that time will tell."

This comes a day after Penguin India released a statement of clarification: "Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish 'Belonging' because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances."

The statement was referring to a report by The Indian Express which said the publishing house would not publish the book in India because "editorial changes and deletions" were turned down by the author.

"As a publisher, it is both our prerogative and our responsibility to fact check and provide authors with recommendations that are in best interests of their books," Penguin India said in its statement, adding that it "remained willing and keen to publish the book."

Skip next section India monitors glaciers after Nepal disaster

India monitors glaciers after Nepal disaster

Days after deadly flash floods triggered by a glacial collapse swept through the Tibet-Nepal border, India stepped up monitoring of the glaciers in its Himalayan region bordering Nepal and China.

Although the exact cause of the collapse remains unclear, global warming has increased the likelihood of such disasters.

"Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbor, and also have a similar geographic situation... we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region," said Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India's Himalayan state of Uttarakhand.

"We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state," he added.

Kaushik's state is one of India's most ecologically sensitive regions with over 1,266 glacial lakes. 

Skip next section Indian Hindu nationalist group's chief set to address thousands in NYC

Indian Hindu nationalist group's chief set to address thousands in NYC

Mohan Bhagwat, the chief of a controversial right-wing Hindu nationalist group in India closely associated with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, is set to address about 5,000 members of Indian American groups in New York City on Saturday. 

The event titled "Universal Oneness Celebration" is being held at the Infosys Theater in Madison Square Garden and is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue.

It is being met with protests, a denunciation from the city's mayor Zohran Mamdani and a call for sanctions by a US panel on religious freedom. 

Bhagwat's link with Modi

Bhagwat is the chief of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for "National Volunteer Organization."

The group describes itself as a "Hindu-centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus. It disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance.

The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization.

Why is the RSS controversial?

In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities.

However, several interfaith and civil rights groups — including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York — have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history.

The US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), a government advisory body, has called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims."

Recently, it called for the US government to impose targeted sanctions on RSS members, including Bhagwat, and Indian officials who support the group.

The Ministry of External Affairs in India quickly rejected the commission’s remarks, calling the body biased and lacking in credibility.

United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more.

Skip next section WATCH: Nepal village buried in mud

WATCH: Nepal village buried in mud

DW correspondent Adil Bhat reports from a village in Nepal's Nuwakot district that was buried in mud after severe flooding.

Skip next section Over 300 Indians still missing in Nepal-Tibet floods

Over 300 Indians still missing in Nepal-Tibet floods

At least 320 Indian nationals were still unaccounted for in the Nepal-Tibet floods as of Friday evening, according to the latest update from India's foreign ministry.

A glacier collapse on Wednesday ‌unleashed a huge torrentof rock, ice, mud and ‌debris ​through Himalayan mountain river systems, killing more than 600 people in Nepal and China's Tibet. Over 2,000 people are missing.

Here's the latest update on Indian nationals:

  • 84 Indian nationals have been rescued so far, including 21 from Tamil Nadu who have returned to India and 63 who were working at the Trishuli-I power project in Nepal
  • 149 crossed over into Nepal from China
  • Around 400 are safe in China, the Indian Embassy in Beijing is working on their evacuation
  • 320 are missing or unreachable

Meanwhile, India dispatched a third flight carrying relief supplies to Nepal on Friday evening. The flight also carried an 11-member medical and tunnel rescue team, who are now working on the ground, according to India's Foreign Minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar.

Skip next section Modi is en route to Uzbekistan for bilateral talks

Modi is en route to Uzbekistan for bilateral talks

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi left for a state visit to Uzbekistan, where he is set to discuss ways of deepening cooperation with President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. 

Ahead of departure, Modi said he looked forward to his discussions with the Uzbek president to "further deepening our cooperation in trade and investment, digital connectivity, defence, energy, and on advancing our shared visions of Viksit Bharat and Yangi Uzbekistan."

"Viksit Bharat" roughly translates to "Developed India" and is a commonly used term by Modi and his ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. "Yangi Uzbekistan" translates to "New Uzbekistan" and is a political slogan used by Mirziyoyev.

On Saturday, Modi will attend a dinner hosted by Mirziyoyev, followed by bilateral engagements with him on Sunday at the Presidential Palace.

After his two-day state visit to Uzbekistan, Modi will travel to the Kyrgyz Republic to attend the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit, where he is also scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting with the Russian President, Vladimir Putin.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello and welcome to DW's India blog!

This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from the Delhi studio and I will be your guide through the chaotic news cycle of the world's most populous nation.

Hundreds of Indians remain missing in the devastating Nepal-Tibet flash floods, as of the Indian foreign ministry's last update. Most of those unaccounted for or stranded were either working in Nepal or were pilgrims visiting the Kailash Mansarovar site in China's Tibet.

Indian embassies in Kathmandu and Beijing are working closely with local authorities, and Delhi has sent at least three tranches of aid.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi embarked on a four-day official trip to Central Asia. He will first visit Uzbekistan to hold bilateral discussions and further cooperation between the two nations. Modi will then attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Kyrgyzstan for the last two days of his tour. 

Stay tuned for all of this and more!

entries.title: Nearly 200,000 forced deportees received by Haiti, UN says
entries.summary: Amid surging gang violence, Haiti received thousands of forced returnees. An emergency meeting of the UN Security Council was called to discuss the situation in Haiti following a deadly gang attack.
entries.content:
Haiti

Nearly 200,000 forced deportees received by Haiti, UN says

August 29, 2026

Amid surging gang violence, Haiti received thousands of forced returnees. An emergency meeting of the UN Security Council was called to discuss the situation in Haiti following a deadly gang attack.

The first eight months of 2026 have seen almost 200,000 people being forcibly returned to Haiti, an emergency meeting of the United Nations Security Council learned on Friday, days after a gang attack near the troubled Caribbean nation's capital left 47 people dead.

The attack — which took place on Sunday in Kenscoff on the outskirts of the capital, Port-au-Prince — came days after a first US deportation flight landed in Haiti following the Trump administration winning a legal case which stripped away the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for thousands of Haitians.

Activists caution that Haiti, at present, is too dangerous amid surging gang violence and lacks the resources to help those being deported to the country.

"The latest attack on Kenscoff is yet another grim reminder of the suffering Haitians face every day," Indrika Ratwatte, the acting UN Assistant Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs, told the Security Council on Friday.

What else was discussed at the UNSC emergency meeting?

Forcible deportations to Haiti so far in 2026 were 10% higher over the same period last year, Ratwatte said.

Meanwhile, nearly 1.5 million people, among Haiti's population of nearly 12 million, are internally displaced, with half of them being children, as per the summary of the Securtiy Council's meeting.

Ratwatte told the UNSC that the displacement has doubled in just two years, while describing the conditions in many displacement sites as "squalid".

Haiti calls for rapid deployment of multinational force

At the meeting, Haiti urged the full deployment of the UN mandated Gang ‌Suppression Force (GSF).

The multinational force was authorized in 2025 to suppress gang violence across Haiti and restore public safety, working alongside the Haitian police and armed forces.

The GSF aims to reach a capacity of 5,500 troops by fall and the Security Council will vote on whether to renew its mandate at the end of next month.

At the UNSC emergency meeting, Haiti's representative Pierre Ericq Pierre called on the international community to accelerate the deployment of the GSF to its planned strength.

US representative Jennifer Locetta urged the Security Council to renew the GSF's mandate.

"The ⁠GSF was not created to issue statements from within a compound wall or spend our money while Haiti suffers," she said.

Locetta said that if more nations ⁠bring material support to the force, ​it could assist police fight gangs more efficiently.

"This attack is precisely why the UN authorized Gang Suppression Force's mission and mandate matters," she said.

Calls for stronger arms embargo in Haiti

Pierre also asked for support for his country's recruitment and training of new military personnel and stronger enforcement of the UNSC's arms embargo to curb the flow of firearms and ammunition.

An illegal flow of weapons and ammunition into Haiti has continued to strengthen armed gangs, according to the UN Human Rights Office.

The UN on Friday referred to reports of a gang operating in Port-au-Prince displaying what appeared to be a new shipment of weapons arriving from abroad on its social media account earlier this week, despite the UNSC arms embargo on Haiti which has been enforced since 2022.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko
